topic: CT chest, abdomen and PET-CT: staging of a lung mass
history: 66 year old woman, ex-smoker, 4 months of cough and weight loss. Chest radiograph reported a right upper zone opacity.
imaging: Study 1: contrast-enhanced CT chest. A 45 mm spiculated soft tissue mass lies in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe with pleural tethering to the adjacent fissure; it does not abut the mediastinal pleura or chest wall and there is no pleural effusion. A right paratracheal (station 4R) node measures 17 mm in short axis and a subcarinal node measures 15 mm; the left hilar and left mediastinal nodes are normal in size. There is mild background emphysema and two 4 mm densely calcified granulomata in the left lung. Study 2: contrast-enhanced CT abdomen. The left adrenal gland contains a 28 mm heterogeneously enhancing nodule with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 HU. The right adrenal, liver, kidneys and pancreas are normal. Study 3: FDG PET-CT. The right upper lobe mass has an SUVmax of 12.4. The 4R and subcarinal nodes are avid (SUVmax 7.1 and 6.3), and the left adrenal nodule is avid (SUVmax 8.0). There is no other abnormal uptake, and the brain is not included in the field.

findings: Spiculated 45 mm mass in the right upper lobe, FDG avid, without chest wall or mediastinal invasion (T2b by size).
Enlarged, FDG avid ipsilateral paratracheal (4R) and subcarinal nodes: multiple ipsilateral mediastinal stations, N2b (TNM 9th edition).
Solitary 28 mm left adrenal nodule, indeterminate on CT (38 HU unenhanced) but FDG avid, suspicious for metastasis.
Mild background emphysema and two small densely calcified left lung granulomata (benign); no pleural effusion.
model_report.diagnosis: Primary lung carcinoma of the right upper lobe with multistation N2b nodal disease and a solitary left adrenal metastasis, clinical stage IVA (cT2b N2b M1b, TNM 9th edition; M1b is a single extrathoracic metastasis in a single organ), pending tissue confirmation.
differential: Lung carcinoma with an incidental lipid-poor left adrenal adenoma and N2b disease: stage IIIB in the 9th edition (IIIA in the 8th edition)
Pulmonary lymphoma or carcinoid with nodal and adrenal spread
Granulomatous infection (tuberculosis, fungal) with FDG avid nodes
model_report.investigation_management: Dedicated MRI or CT brain with contrast to complete staging. Tissue diagnosis: biopsy of the most accessible site that would confirm highest stage, for example adrenal or the 4R/subcarinal nodes by EBUS-TBNA, with histology and molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, PD-L1). Adrenal biopsy or MRI chemical shift is needed to prove the adrenal lesion is a metastasis before it changes treatment intent. Present at a lung cancer multidisciplinary meeting. If metastasis is confirmed, treatment is systemic (targeted therapy or immunotherapy based on biomarkers) with palliative radiotherapy as needed rather than surgery; if the adrenal nodule proves benign, the disease is cT2b N2b M0, stage IIIB (9th edition), and chemoradiotherapy with consolidation immunotherapy is considered.

acceptable_diagnoses: non-small cell lung cancer with adrenal metastasis

Differential: adrenal adenoma, granulomatous disease, lymphoma

topic: MRI brain with contrast: ring-enhancing frontal mass
history: 61 year old man, 5 weeks of progressive headache, personality change and a first generalised seizure. Non-contrast CT showed a frontal mass.
imaging: MRI brain with and without gadolinium including diffusion, perfusion and spectroscopy. A 5.5 cm irregular mass centred in the right frontal lobe white matter extends across the genu of the corpus callosum into the left frontal lobe. On T2 and FLAIR there is extensive surrounding high signal oedema with mass effect, 9 mm of midline shift to the left and effacement of the right frontal horn. After contrast there is thick, nodular and irregular peripheral enhancement around a central non-enhancing region. The central region is T2 hyperintense and shows facilitated diffusion with high ADC. Foci of susceptibility signal within the wall are consistent with blood products. The enhancing rim has a markedly elevated relative cerebral blood volume on perfusion imaging. Spectroscopy shows a raised choline to NAA ratio and a prominent lipid and lactate peak. No other intracranial lesion is seen, and the dura is unaffected. The ventricles are not hydrocephalic.

findings: 5.5 cm right frontal mass crossing the genu of the corpus callosum into the contralateral hemisphere.
Thick irregular nodular peripheral enhancement with a non-enhancing necrotic centre showing facilitated diffusion.
Intralesional susceptibility from haemorrhage and extensive vasogenic oedema with 9 mm midline shift.
Elevated rCBV in the enhancing rim and raised choline to NAA ratio with lipid and lactate.
Solitary lesion, no dural attachment.
model_report.diagnosis: High grade glioma, most likely glioblastoma (IDH wildtype), with butterfly pattern spread across the corpus callosum.
differential: Cerebral abscess (against: facilitated not restricted diffusion in the cavity, no thin smooth rim)
model_report.investigation_management: Systemic staging (CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) if histology is uncertain, to exclude an unrecognised primary. Neurosurgical referral for maximal safe resection with tissue for histology and molecular markers (IDH, MGMT promoter methylation). Postoperative MRI within 48 to 72 hours to assess extent of resection. Dexamethasone for vasogenic oedema and an antiepileptic drug given the presenting seizure. Neuro-oncology multidisciplinary meeting, then radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide.

Diagnosis: glioblastoma or high grade glioma
Differential: metastasis, lymphoma, abscess, demyelination with discriminating feature

Management: surgery, steroids, MDT, chemoradiotherapy

history: 68 year old man, painless jaundice for 2 weeks, 8 kg weight loss and new diabetes. Bilirubin 210 micromol/L.
imaging: CT abdomen, pancreatic protocol, with late arterial and portal venous phases. A 30 mm ill-defined hypoattenuating mass lies in the pancreatic head and uncinate process, with poor enhancement relative to normal parenchyma. The common bile duct is dilated to 14 mm and the main pancreatic duct to 7 mm, both tapering abruptly at the mass, and the gallbladder is distended. The body and tail of the pancreas are atrophic. The mass is in contact with the right lateral wall of the superior mesenteric vein over about 120 degrees, with mild irregularity of the vein contour but a patent lumen. A fat plane is preserved around the superior mesenteric artery and the coeliac axis. The portal vein, splenic vein, common hepatic artery and gastroduodenal artery are free. There are no liver lesions, no ascites and no peritoneal nodularity. A 6 mm portocaval node is present, below size criteria. No para-aortic or aortocaval nodes are enlarged.

findings: 30 mm hypoenhancing mass in the pancreatic head and uncinate process.
Dilated common bile duct (14 mm) and main pancreatic duct (7 mm) with abrupt cut-off, the double duct sign; distended gallbladder; upstream pancreatic atrophy.
Contact with the SMV over about 120 degrees with contour irregularity but patent lumen; no contact with the SMA, coeliac axis or hepatic artery.
Subcentimetre portocaval node only; no para-aortic or aortocaval adenopathy; no liver metastases, ascites or peritoneal disease.
model_report.diagnosis: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the head with biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction, borderline resectable because of SMV involvement of 180 degrees or less with contour irregularity.
model_report.investigation_management: Staging CT chest, serum CA 19-9 (interpreted with bilirubin), and MRI liver if any equivocal lesion. For a borderline resectable tumour neoadjuvant chemotherapy is usually offered before surgery (pancreaticoduodenectomy). Biliary drainage by ERCP with a metal stent is used if surgery is delayed or cholangitis or neoadjuvant therapy is planned.

topic: CT angiogram aorta: tearing chest pain
history: 54 year old man with hypertension, sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a blood pressure difference of 40 mmHg between arms. Troponin mildly raised.
imaging: ECG-gated CT angiogram of the thorax, followed by non-gated CT abdomen and pelvis angiography. Non-contrast images show a crescentic high attenuation in the wall of the ascending aorta. After contrast an intimal flap is seen starting 2 cm above the aortic valve and extending through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta, abdominal aorta and left common iliac artery. The ascending aorta measures 46 mm. The true lumen is compressed in the descending aorta and the false lumen is larger and enhances later. The flap extends into the brachiocephalic trunk, which shows reduced enhancement. The right coronary ostium arises from the true lumen with the flap close to its origin. The coeliac axis and superior mesenteric artery arise from the true lumen. The left renal artery arises from the false lumen and the left kidney enhances less than the right. A small pericardial effusion of 12 mm contains fluid at 45 HU. There is no mediastinal haematoma outside the aortic wall and no pleural effusion.

findings: Intimal flap beginning above the aortic valve and extending from the ascending aorta through the arch to the left common iliac artery, with a 46 mm ascending aorta.
Compressed true lumen distally and a larger, later enhancing false lumen; brachiocephalic involvement with reduced flow.
Left renal artery arising from the false lumen with reduced left renal enhancement (malperfusion); coeliac axis and SMA from the true lumen.
Flap near the right coronary ostium, but ostium arising from true lumen.
Small high attenuation pericardial effusion (haemopericardium) with no mediastinal rupture.
model_report.diagnosis: Acute aortic dissection, Stanford type A (DeBakey type I), with branch vessel malperfusion and a haemopericardium.
differential: Intramural haematoma (crescentic wall thickening without flap)
Pulsation or motion artefact mimicking a flap in the ascending aorta
model_report.investigation_management: Immediate escalation: this is a surgical emergency and the patient should not be delayed for further imaging. Urgent cardiothoracic surgical referral for ascending aortic and hemiarch repair. Intravenous beta blockade for impulse control, then vasodilator, aiming for systolic pressure 100 to 120 mmHg. Transfer to a cardiac surgical centre with cross-matching, and transthoracic or transoesophageal echocardiography to assess the aortic valve and tamponade if the patient is unstable. Pericardiocentesis is avoided unless there is peri-arrest tamponade. Renal malperfusion and cerebral perfusion are assessed during the repair, and follow-up CT surveillance is arranged postoperatively.

Diagnosis: Stanford type A dissection with complications
Differential: IMH, PAU, rupture, artefact
Further investigation: echocardiography, communicate and no further delay
Management: surgery, blood pressure control, avoid pericardiocentesis, transfer

common_errors: Failing to state the Stanford type.
Missing renal malperfusion.
Recommending anticoagulation or thrombolysis.
Not communicating urgently.

topic: Radiograph, MRI and CT chest: adolescent knee pain
history: 15 year old boy, 6 weeks of worsening pain and swelling above the right knee, worse at night. Alkaline phosphatase raised.
imaging: Study 1: right knee radiographs, AP and lateral. In the distal femoral metaphysis there is a mixed sclerotic and lytic lesion with an ill-defined zone of transition. There is aggressive periosteal reaction with a Codman triangle posteriorly and spiculated sunburst new bone formation anteriorly. Cloud-like matrix mineralisation extends into a posterior soft tissue mass. The growth plate is open. Study 2: MRI of the femur with contrast. The lesion measures 11 cm in craniocaudal length with low T1 and heterogeneous T2 signal, extending through the cortex into a 5 cm enhancing soft tissue mass. It crosses the physis into the epiphysis. The neurovascular bundle is displaced but the popliteal artery is not encased. A 2 cm separate focus of marrow abnormality is seen 8 cm proximal to the main lesion within the same bone. The knee joint is not involved. Study 3: CT chest. Three peripheral subpleural nodules in the right lung measure 4 to 9 mm; one has dense internal calcification. There is no effusion.

findings: Aggressive distal femoral metaphyseal lesion with mixed sclerosis and lysis and a wide zone of transition.
Codman triangle, sunburst periosteal reaction and cloud-like osteoid matrix within a soft tissue mass.
MRI: 11 cm intramedullary extent, 5 cm extra-osseous mass, physeal and epiphyseal extension, popliteal artery not encased, separate skip lesion in the same bone.
CT chest: multiple subpleural nodules (one calcified), suspicious for pulmonary metastases.
model_report.diagnosis: Conventional osteosarcoma of the distal femur with a skip lesion and probable pulmonary metastases.
differential: Ewing sarcoma (diaphyseal, permeative, no osteoid matrix)
Telangiectasic osteosarcoma or aneurysmal bone cyst
model_report.investigation_management: Do not biopsy at a peripheral hospital: refer to a sarcoma service first. Image-guided or open biopsy planned by the surgeon so the track can be excised at resection, before any chemotherapy. Whole body staging with PET-CT or bone scintigraphy to find other skeletal lesions, and MRI of the whole femur has already shown the skip lesion. Biopsy of a lung nodule is generally not needed if imaging is typical. Sarcoma multidisciplinary meeting. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (usually methotrexate, doxorubicin and cisplatin), then limb-salvage surgery with wide resection and reconstruction, and resection of pulmonary metastases where possible.

Further investigation: follow-up imaging, cardiac work-up
Management: thrombectomy and thrombolysis decision with DOAC caveat

common_errors: Not reporting ASPECTS.
Ignoring the DOAC when discussing thrombolysis.
Reporting the CTP mismatch without volumes.
Delaying thrombectomy for MRI.

topic: CT enterography: right iliac fossa pain and weight loss
history: 24 year old man, 8 months of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss. Faecal calprotectin raised. Colonoscopy could not reach the terminal ileum.
imaging: CT enterography with neutral oral contrast and enteric phase intravenous contrast. A 12 cm segment of terminal ileum shows concentric mural thickening to 11 mm with mucosal hyperenhancement and a stratified (layered) pattern. The mesenteric border is involved and the vasa recta are prominent (comb sign). There is increased attenuation of the surrounding mesenteric fat with fibrofatty proliferation wrapping the bowel wall. A 4 cm segment at the distal end has a luminal diameter of 6 mm with proximal small bowel dilatation to 3.6 cm and a small bowel faeces sign. A 2 cm ill-defined hypodense collection lies adjacent to the ileocaecal valve with an internal gas locule and a thin track connecting it to an adjacent ileal loop. Several mesenteric nodes up to 9 mm are present. The colon, liver and pancreas are normal. No free fluid or free air.

findings: Long segment terminal ileal mural thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement, layering, comb sign and fibrofatty proliferation.
Short distal stricture with upstream small bowel dilatation (3.6 cm) and small bowel faeces sign.
Small ileocaecal peri-enteric collection with a fistulous track to an adjacent ileal loop (enteroenteric fistula).
Reactive mesenteric nodes; colon and solid organs normal; no perforation.
model_report.diagnosis: Crohn disease of the terminal ileum, active inflammatory, with a stricture, small bowel obstruction features and a penetrating complication (phlegmon or small abscess with enteroenteric fistula).
model_report.investigation_management: MR enterography or repeat ultrasound can separate inflammatory from fibrotic stricture and assess collection size. Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy (or enteroscopy) for histological confirmation, plus stool culture, and tuberculosis testing in an at-risk patient. Gastroenterology and colorectal surgical review at an IBD multidisciplinary meeting. Treat sepsis if present: antibiotics and percutaneous drainage if the collection is greater than 3 cm. Biological therapy for active disease without a fixed fibrotic stricture; surgical resection or stricturoplasty for a symptomatic stricture with penetrating complications.

marking_template.item: Findings: length and wall features, comb sign and fat, stricture with upstream dilatation, collection and fistula
Diagnosis: Crohn disease with complications
Differential: tuberculosis, lymphoma, Yersinia, neoplasm
Further investigation: MR enterography, endoscopic biopsy, TB testing
Management: MDT, drainage and antibiotics, biologic or surgery

common_errors: Not distinguishing inflammatory from fibrostenotic disease.
Omitting the fistula.
Missing small bowel obstruction features.
No mention of tuberculosis in the differential.

history: 71 year old man, 18 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough. Bibasal inspiratory crackles with digital clubbing. Restrictive spirometry with reduced DLCO. Former smoker, no occupational dust exposure, no bird exposure.
imaging: High resolution CT chest, supine inspiratory, with prone and expiratory acquisitions, 1 mm slices. There is subpleural and basal predominant reticulation with traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis. Honeycombing is present in the subpleural zones of both lower lobes, as clustered thick-walled cysts 3 to 10 mm in diameter in several contiguous layers. Mild ground-glass opacity is limited to areas of reticulation. The distribution is relatively sparse in the upper lobes, with the lower zones affected symmetrically. There are no centrilobular nodules, no air trapping on expiratory images and no discrete cysts apart from the honeycombing. There are no well-defined consolidations, pleural plaques or calcified pleura. Mediastinal nodes up to 12 mm are present, with no pleural effusion. A 6 mm solid nodule is noted in the right upper lobe.

findings: Subpleural and basal predominant reticulation with traction bronchiectasis.
Honeycombing in multiple layers at the lung bases.
Limited ground-glass opacity within fibrotic zones; no air trapping, centrilobular nodules or upper lobe predominance.
No pleural plaques; reactive mediastinal nodes; 6 mm right upper lobe nodule needing follow-up per Fleischner.
model_report.diagnosis: Fibrotic interstitial lung disease with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern, in this clinical context consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
differential: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (would show air trapping, centrilobular nodules, upper or mid zone)
model_report.investigation_management: No biopsy is needed when the HRCT shows a UIP pattern in the right clinical context. Review at an ILD multidisciplinary meeting including respiratory physician, radiologist and pathologist. Exclude exposures (birds, mould, drugs such as amiodarone or nitrofurantoin) and test for connective tissue disease with autoantibodies. Full pulmonary function tests and a six minute walk test for baseline. Treat with an antifibrotic (nintedanib or pirfenidone), consider pulmonary rehabilitation and oxygen, and discuss lung transplant referral if suitable. Follow the 6 mm nodule by Fleischner guidance, and watch for lung cancer and acute exacerbation.

marking_template.item: Findings: distribution, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, features excluding alternatives, nodule
Diagnosis: UIP pattern, IPF in context
Differential: HP, CTD-ILD, asbestosis, NSIP
Further investigation: exposures, serology, PFTs, MDT
Management: antifibrotic, rehabilitation, transplant, nodule follow-up

common_errors: Calling fibrosis NSIP despite honeycombing.
Recommending lung biopsy for a UIP pattern.
Missing the lung nodule.
Not mentioning air trapping as the discriminator for HP.

topic: Mammography, ultrasound and MRI breast: screen-detected lesion
history: 54 year old woman recalled from BreastScreen after a screening mammogram. No palpable lump, no family history.
imaging: Study 1: digital mammography with tomosynthesis, right breast CC and MLO. A 22 mm irregular high-density mass with spiculated margins lies in the upper outer quadrant, with architectural distortion. Fine pleomorphic calcifications are grouped within and extend 15 mm beyond the mass in a segmental distribution. A 9 mm lymph node with loss of the fatty hilum is seen in the right axilla. The left breast is normal. Study 2: ultrasound right breast and axilla. A 21 mm irregular, hypoechoic, taller-than-wide mass with an angular margin, posterior acoustic shadowing and an echogenic halo. Colour Doppler shows internal vascularity. A right axillary node has a cortical thickness of 5 mm with absent fatty hilum. Study 3: contrast-enhanced MRI breast. The mass enhances avidly with rapid initial uptake and washout. A separate 6 mm enhancing focus lies 3 cm posterior to the mass in the same quadrant. There is no enhancement in the left breast, no chest wall invasion and no skin thickening.

findings: 22 mm spiculated irregular mass with architectural distortion in the right upper outer quadrant on mammography.
Fine pleomorphic calcifications in a segmental distribution extending beyond the mass.
Ultrasound: irregular hypoechoic taller-than-wide mass with shadowing; axillary node with thickened cortex (5 mm) and absent hilum.
MRI: avid enhancement with washout, a second 6 mm enhancing focus 3 cm away (multifocal disease); chest wall and skin spared; left breast clear.
model_report.diagnosis: Highly suspicious right breast malignancy, likely invasive carcinoma (BI-RADS 5), with suspicious axillary node and a possible second focus.
differential: Radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion (less likely with calcifications and node)
Invasive lobular carcinoma versus ductal carcinoma NST (histological question)
model_report.investigation_management: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the mass with clip placement, and core biopsy or FNA of the abnormal axillary node. Biopsy of the 6 mm MRI focus (second look ultrasound or MRI-guided) if it would alter surgery. Histology with ER, PR and HER2. Multidisciplinary meeting. Treatment depends on pathology: breast conserving surgery versus mastectomy given multifocality, axillary surgery or neoadjuvant systemic therapy for node-positive disease, followed by radiotherapy. Bilateral staging is complete with normal left breast; systemic staging imaging is not routinely needed for early disease unless symptomatic or high stage.

acceptable_diagnoses: breast carcinoma with axillary node involvement

marking_template.item: Findings: mass morphology, calcifications, axillary node, MRI extent and second focus, assessment category
Diagnosis: BI-RADS 5 breast carcinoma, likely invasive
Differential: radial scar, fat necrosis, phyllodes or lymphoma, ILC vs NST
Further investigation: core biopsy with clip, node sampling, MRI-focus biopsy, receptor status
Management: MDT and treatment depending on pathology

common_errors: Not assigning a BI-RADS category.
Missing the second focus on MRI.
Ignoring the abnormal axillary node.
Recommending FNA of the breast mass instead of core biopsy.
